commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-level-7'
Add DateTime to Deadlines.java
Add date formatting to Event class
Merge branch 'branch-level-8'
Align dates in hints, docs and tests with the ISO format
commitResults.messageBody:
The recent commits that gave Deadlines and Event a LocalDate made
yyyy-mm-dd the only accepted date format, but the surrounding text was
never updated with them. The error hints still suggested "/by Sunday"
and "/from Mon 2pm /to 4pm" -- input the parser now rejects -- so a user
who followed the hint got a second error rather than a working command.
The README examples and the text-UI test plan had the same stale dates,
which left TC9 failing against a correct program.

This commit brings all three in line with the parser:

* DavidGoggins.java: the deadline and event hints now suggest real
  yyyy-mm-dd dates.
* README.md: the command table shows the accepted format explicitly, and
  the worked example and save-file sample use ISO dates.
* test/ui-test-plan.md: the test cases feed ISO dates and expect them
  back. The expected hint text was updated to match the new hints, not
  the other way round.

Doing this first gives a green baseline (24/24) to refactor against, so
that any later failure is caused by the refactoring rather than
inherited from before it.

Also commits the text-UI test plan, its runner improvements and the
README command reference, which were still sitting uncommitted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Ui class for all console interaction
commitResults.messageBody:
DavidGoggins was doing two unrelated jobs: deciding what each command
means, and deciding how the chatbot looks on screen. The banner, the
60-character divider, the "OOPS!" error prefix, the Scanner and the reply
layout all sat in the same class as the command handling, so a change to
the wording of a reply and a change to the logic of a command touched the
same file for no reason.

Ui now owns that second job. It holds the banner and divider, prints the
greeting, the reply blocks and the sign-off, and also reads the user's
input -- reading and replying are two halves of the same conversation, so
splitting them across two classes would have been an arbitrary line.

What changed in DavidGoggins:

* reply(), greet() and farewell() moved to Ui as show(), showWelcome()
  and showFarewell(); NAME, DIVIDER and BANNER moved with them.
* The Scanner is gone; the loop now asks ui.hasNextCommand() and
  ui.readCommand(). readCommand() trims, so every command gets the same
  treatment rather than the loop remembering to do it.
* The catch block calls ui.showError(e.getMessage()) instead of building
  " OOPS! " + message itself, so the error format is decided in one place.
* try-with-resources became try/finally around the loop, because ui is a
  field rather than a local. The guarantee is the same: input is released
  even if a command fails unexpectedly.

Ui is instantiated as a field rather than being all-static, so that it is
ready to become a constructor-injected collaborator when the main class
is converted to the instance-based shape in a later step. Storage and
Parser are not touched yet; this step is deliberately limited to the
input/output boundary.

Verified with the text-UI test plan: all 24 test cases pass, so no output
changed by a single character.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Storage class for the save file
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList was doing two jobs at once. Roughly half of it was about a list
of tasks -- add, mark, remove, numbering -- and the other half was about a
file: a Path, a temporary file, an atomic move with a fallback, and three
different ways a load can go wrong. The two have nothing to do with each
other, and a reader looking for how "mark 2" works had to scroll past
NoSuchFileException to find it.

Storage now owns the file half, and is the only class that knows a file
is involved at all:

* save(List<Task>), load(), replace() and deleteIfPresent() moved across
  unchanged; the Path moved with them and is now given to the constructor
  as "data/tasks.txt" rather than hard-coded, so a caller can point the
  chatbot at a different file.
* load() returns the tasks it managed to read instead of filling a list
  in place, which is what lets TaskList be constructed from them.

TaskList keeps its save() method, but it is now one line that hands the
list to Storage. The call stays inside add/mark/unmark/remove rather than
moving out to the command handlers: that keeps "the save file matches the
list" true by construction, whereas five call sites that each have to
remember to save is five chances to lose the user's change. Storage still
knows nothing about TaskList -- it takes a plain List<Task>.

TaskList also gained two constructors: one that loads from Storage, and
one that takes a list directly so it can be built in a test without
touching the disk.

This also closes the gap left by the previous commit. The save and load
warnings used to be printed by TaskList with System.out.println, which
was the last user-facing output not going through Ui. Storage now reports
them with ui.showWarning(), so the " Warning: " label is defined once
alongside the " OOPS! " one. showWarning prints a bare line rather than a
divider block, matching the existing output: the message appears before
the greeting, where a reply block would look like an answer to a command
the user never typed.

The load now happens while the static fields are initialised rather than
in the first line of main(). Fields are initialised in the order written,
so the warning still comes before the banner, and the explicit
tasks.load() call was no longer needed.

Verified with the text-UI test plan: all 24 test cases pass, including
TC22, which checks the skipped-lines warning.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Parser class for reading the user's input
commitResults.messageBody:
DavidGoggins still held two kinds of code side by side: rules about what
counts as valid input ("a deadline needs a /by part", "a task number must
be a whole number", "a description cannot contain a bar") and decisions
about what to do with a valid command. The first kind is what the Parser
is for.

Moved into Parser, with the bodies unchanged:

* handleCommand's two lines of splitting became parseCommand() and
  parseArgument(). parseCommand lower-cases, so LIST and list are the
  same command without every caller remembering it; the argument keeps
  the case the user typed, so a description is stored as written.
* rejectSeparator() moved as it stands.
* The Integer.parseInt block that setDone and deleteTask each had became
  parseTaskNumber(argument, commandName). The command name is a parameter
  so the advice still names the command the user actually typed.
* addTodo, addDeadline and addEvent became parseTodo, parseDeadline and
  parseEvent. They were already "check the argument, then build the
  task"; they now return the task instead of adding it, so the adding is
  left to the caller and the parser has no opinion about the list.

What stayed behind is the part that is genuinely about running a command:
the switch that maps a command word to a task-list operation, and the
handlers that ask TaskList to change and then ask Ui to confirm. The
switch now reads as pure dispatch, e.g.

    case "todo" -> addTask(Parser.parseTodo(Parser.rejectSeparator(argument)));

Two checks deliberately did not move. The "which task number?" check for
an empty argument stayed in setDone and deleteTask, because the two
commands word it differently. The range check stayed too, because whether
task 7 exists depends on the list, and the parser is kept ignorant of the
list on purpose -- the same input always parses the same way, which is
also why every Parser method is static.

DavidGoggins is down to 177 lines from the 341 it started at.

Verified with the text-UI test plan: all 24 test cases pass, so every
error message is still worded and triggered exactly as before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Make DavidGoggins an object rather than a bag of static methods
commitResults.messageBody:
The three collaborators were static fields initialised where they were
declared, which worked but said the wrong thing: it made "there is
exactly one chatbot, wired to exactly one file, decided at class-load
time" a fact about the program rather than a choice anyone made. It also
meant the wiring happened as a side effect of the class being loaded,
which is an awkward place to explain or to change.

DavidGoggins is now an ordinary object:

* ui, storage and tasks became instance fields, assigned in a new
  DavidGoggins(String filePath) constructor. The order there is forced by
  the dependencies and is worth reading as documentation: Storage reports
  a bad save file through the Ui, and TaskList loads itself through the
  Storage.
* The body of main() became run(). main() is now one line --
  new DavidGoggins(FILE_PATH).run() -- so where the tasks live is a
  decision made in the class that assembles the program, not one buried
  in the class that does the saving.
* The command handlers lost their "static": they work on this object's
  task list, so being instance methods is what they always meant.

Loading still happens before the greeting, because the constructor runs
before run() does, so a warning about the save file still appears above
the banner rather than in the middle of the conversation.

That finishes the extraction the exercise asked for. The main class no
longer prints, no longer parses and no longer touches a file; it decides
which task-list operation each command maps to and what to say
afterwards. It ends at 200 lines, from 341 before the first step, with
Ui, Storage and Parser holding the parts that moved out.

Verified with the text-UI test plan: all 24 test cases pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Organise the classes into packages under src/main/java
commitResults.messageBody:
Every class lived in the default package, which cannot be imported from
elsewhere, so no class could be split off without moving all of them.

The packages follow the responsibilities already separated in the previous
commits: task holds the data model (Task, its three subclasses and TaskList),
while parser, storage and ui each hold the one class that knows about the
input format, the file and the console respectively. DavidGoggins and
DavidGogginsException stay at the root because every layer uses them.

Imports were added only where a class crosses a package boundary; the
{@link TaskList} in Storage's class comment is now fully qualified, since
Storage has no code reason to import it and an unused import would be flagged.
No access modifiers needed widening -- the members used across the new
boundaries were already public.

Also includes Javadoc shortening in the affected files that was pending in
the working tree.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a skill for the SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The project requires Java code to follow the SE-EDU Java coding
standard, but nothing in the repository records what that standard says.

An unwritten standard gets applied inconsistently, and a reviewer cannot
point at a rule to justify a comment.

Let's capture the basic and intermediate rules as a project skill, and
have AGENTS.md require it for all Java work in this repository.

The rules are grouped as naming, layout, statements and comments to
match the source guide, and the skill closes with grep and awk checks so
violations can be found mechanically rather than by eye.

Source:
https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/java/intermediate.html

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a skill for the SE-EDU Git conventions
commitResults.messageBody:
Commit messages and branch names must follow the SE-EDU Git conventions,
but the repository records only a one-line reminder to explain the
rationale for a change.

With the rules unwritten, commit messages drift from the conventions the
project is assessed against.

Let's capture the conventions as a project skill, and have AGENTS.md
require it for every commit message and branch name.

The skill grades each rule basic, intermediate or advanced as the source
page does, and reproduces the three worked examples verbatim: they show
a register that the body template alone does not convey.

The existing rules on lightweight tags and on not committing without
being asked are kept, since the SE-EDU page covers neither.

Source: https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/git.html

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Show restored tasks at start-up and fix code style
commitResults.messageBody:
The greeting says nothing about the tasks loaded from the save file, so
a returning user cannot tell whether their list survived the last run
without typing list. Separately, parts of the code break the SE-EDU
Java coding standard that the project follows.

A silent restore leaves the user guessing, and style drift makes the
code harder to read.

Let's,
* print the restored list after the welcome message, skipping it when
  the list is empty so a first run does not announce a list the user
  has not started yet
* indent switch case labels one level inside their switch
* wrap the four over-long event error messages under 120 characters
* add the missing space in the Event class declaration
* put a space after // in trailing comments
* remove blank lines that open a method body, and one trailing space

Only the first bullet changes behaviour; the parser tests still pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a find command for searching tasks by keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
A user with a long list has no way to pull up the few tasks they care
about. The only way to see a task is list, which prints everything.

Searching by keyword lets the list grow without becoming unusable.

Let's add a find command that shows the tasks whose description contains
a keyword, matched without regard to case so the user need not remember
the capitals they first typed.

The search lives on TaskList and the matching test on Task itself, so
the description stays private rather than being exposed through a
getter. The numbering used by list is pulled out into a shared method so
the results are numbered the same way, from 1.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tests for the find command
commitResults.messageBody:
The find command has no tests, so nothing pins down case-insensitive
matching or the numbering of the results.

Those two are the parts most likely to be broken by a later change, and
both are cheap to test: searching reads the list without touching disk.

Let's add TaskListTest for the search and the numbering, and cover
Parser.parseKeyword in the existing ParserTest.

The list under test is built through the constructor that takes its
tasks directly, so no save file is read or written.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Merge branch 'branch-Level-9'
Task: mark toString as an override
commitResults.messageBody:
The abstract toString() gives no sign that it overrides
Object.toString(), so a reader has to know Object's API to see that
subclasses redeclare an inherited method rather than invent one.

Let's annotate it with @Override, which also makes the compiler check
that the signature still matches the method it overrides.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a JavaFX GUI for the chatbot
commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot can only be driven from a terminal, and a conversation
longer than a screen scrolls away.

A window with a scrolling transcript and an input box is easier to use
and keeps the whole exchange in view.

Let's add a JavaFX GUI, built from FXML, that sends each typed line to
the existing chatbot and shows the reply as a dialog bubble.

The GUI reaches the same handleCommand the text UI uses, through a new
getResponse that asks the Ui to collect a reply rather than print it, so
the two interfaces cannot disagree about what a command does. The text
UI is kept because the logic is far easier to test through it than
through the GUI; run it with ./gradlew runText.

Launching goes through a separate Launcher that does not extend
Application, without which JavaFX refuses to start from a shaded JAR.
The JavaFX dependencies follow the tutorial's build.gradle, naming all
three platform classifiers so the build works on any OS.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Restore coding standard fixes lost in the A-CodingStandard merge
commitResults.messageBody:
Three fixes made on the A-CodingStandard branch are absent from master:
the switch in handleCommand has its case labels back at the same indent
as the switch, two of its comments lost the space after the slashes, and
Event's class declaration lost the space before its brace.

The conflict resolution for that merge took the master side of those
hunks, so the increment is only partly applied and the code no longer
matches the standard the project committed to.

Let's put the three back, exactly as the branch had them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-level-10'
Use varargs to build the save-file lines
commitResults.messageBody:
Every Task subclass builds its save line by hand, repeating the type
marker, the done flag, the description and the separators between them.
The three differ only in how many extra fields follow: none for a todo,
one for a deadline, two for an event.

Writing the shared part out three times lets the three drift apart, and
a separator missed in one of them corrupts only that task type, which is
the kind of fault a save file hides until the next reload.

Let's pull the shared part into Task.toSaveFormat, taking the extra
fields as varargs so each subclass passes only the fields it has.

Varargs fits better than an array or a list here because the number of
fields is fixed and known at each call site, so a caller names its
fields directly instead of wrapping them first.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: DavidGoggins: Extract task-number validation into one method
commitResults.messageBody:
The mark, unmark and delete commands each pick a task by number. Both
setDone() and deleteTask() contain an identical copy of the code that
parses that number, checks it against the list size, and builds the
"There's no task N in your list" error with its advice.

Copy-paste-modify code is a code quality problem: any change to the
range rule or the error wording must be made in every copy, and the
copies can silently drift apart so that commands disagree about how a
bad number is reported.

Let's extract the duplicated block into a single private helper,
parseExistingTaskNumber(), that both commands call.

The helper stays in DavidGoggins rather than moving to Parser, because
the range check depends on the task list, which Parser deliberately
knows nothing about. The empty-argument checks stay in each caller,
since their messages differ per command. Every error message is kept
character for character.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Task: Pull the done-status icon up into the parent class
commitResults.messageBody:
Todo, Deadlines and Event each build their display line with the same
inline expression, (isDone ? "[X] " : "[ ] "), copied into all three
toString() methods.

The status icon is behaviour shared by every task, so repeating it in
each subclass is duplicated code: changing the icon (e.g. to a tick)
means editing three classes, and a new task type must remember to copy
it again. It also mixes a low-level detail into lines that otherwise
describe each task at a higher level.

Let's add getStatusIcon() to Task and call it from the subclasses.

The method sits next to the parent's existing doneFlag(), the save-file
counterpart of the same field, so both renderings of isDone live in one
place. The output is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Task: Share one date parser between Deadlines and Event
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadlines and Event each declare their own yyyy-MM-dd formatter and
their own try/catch that turns a DateTimeParseException into the same
"I need the date as yyyy-mm-dd" error. The two formatters are identical
but are named differently: DISPLAY_FORMATTER in Deadlines and
INPUT_FORMATTER in Event, even though each is used only for input.

This is duplicated code with misleading names. A reader seeing two
names assumes two different formats, and changing the accepted date
format or its error wording means finding and editing both copies.

Let's move the formatter and the parsing into a single protected
parseDate() in Task, named DATE_FORMATTER, and have both subclasses
call it. Each subclass passes its own example command, so the error
still suggests a command of the right type.

Task is the natural home because it is the common parent of both dated
tasks; a separate date utility class would be more than two callers
need. Every error message is kept character for character.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename Deadlines class to Deadline
commitResults.messageBody:
The task type for something due by a date is named Deadlines, while
its siblings are named Todo and Event.

A class name should be a singular noun describing one instance, and
each Deadlines object holds exactly one task. The plural name suggests
a collection of deadlines, which misleads readers (e.g. a variable
"Deadlines deadline" reads as a type mismatch), and it is inconsistent
with the naming of the other task types.

Let's rename the class and its file to Deadline, and update every
reference in the main code and the tests.

This is a pure rename with no change in behaviour or save-file format,
since the saved type marker is "D" rather than the class name.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: DavidGoggins: Rename taskCount() to formatTaskCount()
commitResults.messageBody:
The helper that words the list size for a sentence ("1 task",
"2 tasks") is named taskCount().

Methods should be named with verbs, and things with nouns. The noun
name taskCount() reads like it returns a number, the same value as
tasks.size(), when it actually builds a phrase with the correct
plural. A reader at the call site cannot tell the difference without
opening the method.

Let's rename it to formatTaskCount(), a verb phrase that says the
method produces display text rather than a count.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove comments that repeat what the code says
commitResults.messageBody:
Several trailing comments restate the line they sit on, e.g.
"// user did not provide a /to part" beside a check that the /to split
failed, "// set the argument (number) task as done" beside
setDone(argument, true), and "// split the input into at most two
parts" directly under a comment already explaining the split limit.

Comments should explain what and why, not repeat what well-named code
already shows. Such comments add reading effort without adding
information, and they tend to rot: nothing forces them to change when
the code beside them does.

Let's delete these comments in Parser and DavidGoggins, keeping the
ones that explain intent or a non-obvious choice.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Parser: Replace repeated example commands with named constants
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser's error messages end with a sample command showing the correct
syntax. The same literal is typed out in full in every message for its
task type: the event example appears five times and the deadline
example three times. Some of these lines exceed the 120-character
limit.

These are magic literals. Changing a sample (e.g. updating its date)
means finding every copy, and a missed copy leaves the chatbot
suggesting inconsistent syntax for the same command.

Let's define TODO_EXAMPLE, DEADLINE_EXAMPLE and EVENT_EXAMPLE once and
build each message from them.

The constants stay private to Parser because the messages that use
them are all here. The resulting messages are unchanged character for
character.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Ui: Extract the GUI capture branch out of show()
commitResults.messageBody:
show() serves both interfaces. Its first branch collects a reply for
the GUI, looping over the arguments and then over the lines inside
each one, three levels deep. Its second branch prints the same reply
to the console between dividers.

Mixing the two means the method works at two levels of abstraction at
once: the console path reads as "print a block", while the GUI path
is line-splitting and whitespace detail. The nesting hides the happy
path, and a reader must get through the inner loop before reaching the
console output that most callers produce.

Let's move the GUI branch into a private capture() method, leaving
show() as a short choice between capturing and printing.

The explanation of why dividers and leading spaces are dropped moves
into capture()'s header comment, where it describes the whole method.
Neither the console nor the GUI output changes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Main: Name the window title and minimum size as constants
commitResults.messageBody:
start() sets up the stage with bare literals: the title string and the
numbers 480.0 and 440.0 passed to setMinHeight() and setMinWidth().

These are magic literals. A reader has to infer from the method name
that 480.0 is a height in pixels, and the values cannot be found or
adjusted without scanning the body of start() for them.

Let's declare WINDOW_TITLE, MIN_WINDOW_HEIGHT and MIN_WINDOW_WIDTH at
the top of the class and use them in start().

The window looks and behaves exactly as before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add missing header comments and fix an outdated example
commitResults.messageBody:
Task.markAsDone() and TaskList.remove() are public but have no header
comment, although their siblings markAsNotDone(), mark() and unmark()
do. Event.toSaveFormat() has neither a comment nor the blank line that
separates it from toString(). Deadline's comment gives the saved form
as "D | 0 | return book | Sunday", but the due date is now stored as a
yyyy-MM-dd date, so that line can no longer appear in a save file.

Every public method should say what it does for other programmers,
and a comment that contradicts the code is worse than none: a reader
trusting the Deadline example would expect free-text dates to load.

Let's add the missing comments, following the style of the matching
methods, correct the Deadline example to a real saved line, and
restore the blank line in Event.

Only comments and whitespace change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Use streams to filter and format task lists
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList.find(), TaskList.format() and Storage.save() each walk a list
of tasks with a hand-written loop that builds up a result: find() adds
matching tasks to a new list, format() appends numbered lines with a
manual check to avoid a leading separator, and save() appends one save
line per task.

Each loop mixes what the method wants (keep the matching tasks, join
the lines) with the bookkeeping of how to get it. The separator check
in format() in particular is easy to get wrong.

Let's express these as stream pipelines: filter() and collect() for
find(), IntStream.range() with Collectors.joining() for format(), and
map() with Collectors.joining() for save().

format() streams over positions rather than tasks because each line
needs its 1-based number. Storage.load() keeps its loop, because
Task.fromSaveFormat() throws a checked exception, which lambdas cannot
propagate cleanly. The loops in Ui are also kept, as they only print
and read more simply as loops.

Output and save-file contents are unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add help command with a separate GUI help window
commitResults.messageBody:
New users have no way inside the app to discover the commands or their
syntax. The only list is the tail of the unknown-command error, which
had already gone out of date once.

Let's,
* add a help command that lists every command with its syntax, plus an
  example for each command that adds a task; anything typed after
  help is rejected
* open the help page in one reusable, non-modal GUI window owned by
  the main window, and confirm it in the chat
* end the greeting with a pointer to help, and make the unknown-command
  error point to help instead of listing commands
* restyle both windows in a brutalist look (dotted yellow backdrop,
  outlined cream cards, hard shadows, round avatars) and replace both
  avatar images, as requested, since the old text was hard to read

The help examples reuse Parser's example constants, now public, so the
help page and the error messages cannot suggest different syntax. The
help text lives beside the command switch in DavidGoggins, so adding a
command and documenting it happen in the same file.

The UI test plan's greeting snippet and TC10 are updated, and new cases
cover help, HELP and help with details. TC10, TC20, TC22 and TC23 were
already failing because the plan predated the find command and the
start-up task list; their expected output is brought up to date. The
user guide gains a help section. The save format is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge pull request #5 from yjenexd/C-Help
commitResults.messageBody: Add help command with a separate GUI help window

commitResults.messageTitle: Give the chatbot a consistent David Goggins personality
commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot is named David Goggins, but its voice is uneven: some
replies are generic ("Got it. I've added this task:", "OOPS!"), while
others add "you log!" in places that read as typos rather than
character.

A consistent personality makes the app more memorable and matches its
name, banner and STAY HARD button.

Let's give every reply the same tough-love voice:
* a Goggins greeting and farewell
* "NO EXCUSES!" as the error prefix instead of "OOPS!"
* reworded add, mark, unmark, delete, find and empty-list replies
* a progress callout under list, e.g. "2 of 5 done. You're not
  finished."
* error messages that stay in character but still say exactly what to
  type, keeping the tested key phrases

The wording is fixed rather than picked at random, so both the text-UI
test plan and the JUnit tests stay deterministic. The yellow brutalist
palette is kept.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Make the GUI asymmetric, highlight errors and fit any window size
commitResults.messageBody:
Both speakers are shown the same way: equal 60px avatars and bubbles
capped at 270px inside a row fixed at 440px wide. Errors look like any
other reply.

The conversation is between a user and an app, so mirroring the two
sides wastes space, and the fixed widths leave most of a resized window
empty. An error the user skims past is also an error they repeat.

Let's,
* show the user's command as a compact right-aligned chip with no
  avatar, and each reply as a full-width card with a 32px avatar
* show errors as a red card with a "NO EXCUSES!" tag and a brief shake
* set task lines in a monospace font so the [T][X] boxes line up
* drop the fixed widths so bubbles re-wrap as the window is resized,
  tighten the margins, and lower the minimum window size to 340x360

DavidGoggins remembers whether its last reply was an error, rather than
the GUI searching the reply's words, so rewording a message cannot break
the highlighting. In the GUI the error prefix moves out of the text and
into the tag; the text UI still prints it.

The design is original; no past project was used as a reference.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Refuse duplicate tasks, impossible dates and malformed flags
commitResults.messageBody:
Several kinds of bad input are accepted or explained misleadingly:
* 2026-02-30 is quietly stored as 2026-02-28, because the date
  formatter resolves dates "smartly" rather than strictly
* the same task can be added any number of times
* a repeated /by, a /from in a deadline or /to before /from is
  reported as a bad date or a missing part, not as the real problem
* "list all" silently lists, and "bye now" is called an unknown command
* "mark 1 2" and a number too large for an int are both called "not a
  task number"

Each of these either corrupts the list or sends the user looking in
the wrong place for their mistake.

Let's,
* parse dates strictly, with separate advice for a real-looking date
  that does not exist
* refuse a task that duplicates one in the list, comparing type,
  description (ignoring case and extra spaces) and dates, but not
  whether it is done
* name repeated, misplaced and unknown flags, and /to before /from
* refuse details after list and bye, and several task numbers at once

A one-day event stays valid: dates carry no time, so "start before
end" cannot be required. Past dates are still accepted, so overdue
work can be logged. A todo only rejects the date flags, since other
slash-words, e.g. a path, are likely meant.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Protect the save file and surface problems the user cannot see
commitResults.messageBody:
When the save file is damaged, its unreadable lines are dropped at the
next save with no copy kept. When it cannot be read at all, e.g. for
lack of permission, the next save replaces it with the empty list that
loading produced. Messages for such errors often show only a file name.
In the GUI, load warnings go to a console the user never sees, and an
unexpected exception in a command escapes to JavaFX, leaving the reply
missing.

These are the moments a user is most likely to lose tasks without
knowing why.

Let's,
* copy a damaged or unreadable save file to tasks.txt.bak before it can
  be overwritten, and refuse to save over a file that could neither be
  read nor copied
* describe common file errors in plain words, e.g. "permission denied"
* show load warnings in the GUI as a yellow HEADS UP card
* catch unexpected RuntimeExceptions in both UIs, showing a short
  apology and logging the stack trace to standard error

Assertion errors are left uncaught, so a broken invariant still stops
the program during development.

Manually checked with a corrupt file, a binary file, a file without
read permission, a folder in place of the file, and a file in place of
the data folder.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Test nearly all non-GUI code and measure the coverage
commitResults.messageBody:
The JUnit tests cover only Parser#parseDeadline, Parser#parseKeyword
and TaskList#find: about 18% of the lines outside the GUI. DavidGoggins,
Storage, Ui and Event have no tests, and nothing shows what is missed.
The text-UI plan has no case for find or the progress callouts.

Untested code is where later changes break things unnoticed, and file
handling is the part most likely to cost a user their tasks.

Let's,
* add JaCoCo, so "./gradlew test jacocoTestReport" reports coverage
  of every class except the JavaFX ones, which are tested by hand
* add junit-jupiter-params, so one test can run over many bad inputs
* add tests for Task, Event, TaskList, Parser, Storage, Ui and
  DavidGoggins, raising coverage to 93.5% of lines and 90% of branches
* add text-UI cases for find, the progress callouts and rewriting a
  damaged save file
* default the text-UI runner to davidgoggins.DavidGoggins, the class
  that actually exists, so it runs without extra arguments

Storage is tested against real files in a JUnit @TempDir rather than a
fake, since what matters is how it copes with the file system itself.
The permission test is skipped where permissions are not enforced, e.g.
on Windows or when run as root.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Lower-case input the same way whatever the machine's language
commitResults.messageBody:
Command words, search keywords and duplicate checks are lower-cased
with the machine's default locale. In a Turkish locale, "I" lower-cases
to a dotless "ı", so LIST is rejected as the unknown command "lıst" and
"find lift" misses a task named "LIFT weights".

This was found by running the app with different language settings,
as part of manual testing.

Let's lower-case with Locale.ROOT, which applies the same rules on
every machine, and add regression tests that switch the default locale
to Turkish.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Record the manual GUI and environment tests
commitResults.messageBody:
The GUI classes are excluded from the coverage report because they are
tested by hand, but the hand testing is not written down anywhere, so
nobody can repeat it or see what was left unchecked.

Let's add docs/manual-testing.md, listing each GUI and environment
check with its steps, expected result and outcome, plus what still
needs a Windows or Linux machine to check.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: User guide and UI.png
Merge branch 'A-Personality'
commitResults.messageBody:
The chatbot greets, confirms and refuses in plain, neutral wording that
could belong to any task tracker.

A chatbot named after David Goggins should sound like him, so the
persona belongs in every message the user can see rather than in the
name alone.

Let's bring in A-Personality, which rewrites the greeting, the
confirmations, the progress line and the error messages in one
consistent voice, and adds an ASCII banner to match.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'A-BetterGui'
commitResults.messageBody:
Both sides of the conversation are drawn the same way, errors look like
ordinary replies, and the window assumes one fixed size.

A user cannot tell at a glance who said what, or which replies were
refusals, and the window is awkward on a screen of a different size.

Let's bring in A-BetterGui, which makes the two speakers visually
distinct, marks errors with their own colour and label, and lets the
layout follow the window.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'A-MoreErrorHandling'
commitResults.messageBody:
Bad input slips through in several places: a duplicate task is accepted,
an impossible date such as 30 February is taken as real, a repeated flag
is swallowed into a date, and a save that fails does so silently.

Each of these leaves the user with a list that is wrong, or unreadable
on the next run, without ever telling them why.

Let's bring in A-MoreErrorHandling, which refuses duplicates, malformed
dates and repeated flags with advice naming the command at fault, and
reports save-file trouble instead of overwriting a file it could not
read.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'A-MoreTesting'
commitResults.messageBody:
Testing covers a handful of classes, the GUI and the packaged JAR are
checked only by hand with no record of what was tried, and the user
guide is still the template stub.

Without a written plan, a manual test cannot be repeated by anyone else,
and a user given only the stub has nothing to work from.

Let's bring in A-MoreTesting, which adds unit tests across nearly all
non-GUI code with coverage measured, records the manual GUI and
environment tests, fixes case handling that depended on the machine's
language, and replaces the stub user guide with the real one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Ui.png
Warn when marking a task that is already in that state
commitResults.messageBody:
The mark and unmark commands confirm success even when the task is
already done (or not done), so the user gets no hint that the command
changed nothing. A smoke tester reported this as confusing.

Let's show a warning instead and leave the task and save file alone.
The GUI shows it in the yellow warning card, which already exists for
save-file warnings, so the reply is visibly different from a normal
confirmation without being styled as an error.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Reject dates with years outside 1900 to 2100
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline and event dates accept any year the formatter can parse, so a
typo such as 0026-10-15 is stored as a real date. A smoke tester
reported that unrealistically old years are accepted.

Let's reject years before 1900 or after 2100 with a message naming the
allowed range. A fixed range is simple and generous enough for any real
task. Refusing past dates was not chosen, as it would stop saved tasks
from loading once their dates have passed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix chat scrolling freezing after the window is resized
commitResults.messageBody:
The scroll position of the conversation is bound to the height of the
dialog container, so that new messages stay in view. A bound property
cannot be set by anything else, so scrolling by the user fights the
binding. A smoke tester found that scrolling froze after a resize until
the window lost and regained focus.

Let's use a listener that moves to the bottom whenever the conversation
grows, instead of a binding. New messages still scroll into view, and
the user remains free to scroll in between.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
